definition: Quick to understand a situation and use that understanding to your advantage.
example: The astute coach saw the other team tiring in the final minutes and told her players to speed up the game.
nuance: Astute praises practical sharpness in reading a situation, while shrewd can hint at self-serving cunning.
prompt: A shop owner notices that customers keep lingering near the front window.
options: The astute owner moved the best-selling scarves into the window display.
The astute owner never noticed which items customers paused to look at.
After rearranging the window, the owner felt an astute pain in her lower back.
The astute owner rearranged the window at random and hoped something would sell.
reasons: She read what shoppers were drawn to and turned that insight into more sales.
Missing an obvious clue about customers is the reverse of sharp perception.
This confuses the word with acute, which describes sharp or sudden pain.
Guessing at random shows no insight into the situation at all.

practice.prompt: A student is preparing for a debate against a skilled opponent.
options: The astute debater accepted every claim his opponent made without asking for any evidence.
The astute debater studied her rival's past speeches and prepared a reply to each tactic.
The astute debater skipped all preparation, assuming the judges would simply favor him over his rival.
The debater was so astute by her opponent's opening that she dropped her note cards.
reasons: Believing everything without question is naive, the opposite of sharp judgment.
Anticipating an opponent's moves and planning for them shows keen practical insight.
Careless overconfidence ignores the real situation instead of reading it well.
This mistakes the word for astounded; it describes cleverness, not shock.
